title: Estimating Prevalence and Risk Ratios Directly

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A risk-ratio (or prevalence-ratio) regression models a binary outcome with a log link: log(p) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + … Then exp(b) is an adjusted risk ratio (RR) in a cohort, or prevalence ratio (PR) in a cross-sectional survey. There are two ways to fit it:

  • Log-binomial regression: binomial distribution, log link.
  • Modified Poisson regression: Poisson “family”, log link, with a robust (sandwich) standard error (Zou, 2004).

A robust (sandwich) standard error is an SE computed from the observed spread of the residuals instead of from the variance the model assumes. It stays valid when the model’s variance assumption is wrong, provided the model for the mean is right.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
When an outcome is common, the OR exaggerates the RR (recall §13.2.6). The more common the outcome, the more the OR overstates an RR above 1 or understates one below 1 (Zhang & Yu, 1998). CBHI membership (30%), anaemia in women, or full immunisation coverage are all common. A cross-sectional community survey should usually report prevalence ratios.

Log-binomial regression is the natural model, but the log link does not keep p below 1. The fitting algorithm must stay inside the region where every predicted p < 1, and it often fails to converge (McNutt et al., 2003).

Modified Poisson regression fits the same log-link model for the mean, using the Poisson likelihood as a working device. A 0/1 outcome is not a Poisson count: its variance is p(1 − p), smaller than the Poisson’s p. The coefficients are still valid estimates of log PRs; only the model-based SEs are wrong (too large). The sandwich SE fixes them (Zou, 2004).

A third option is marginal standardisation: fit the logistic model, predict every household’s probability as if all were exposed, then as if none were, and divide the two averages. This gives an adjusted RR (or, by subtraction, a risk difference) on the probability scale.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Converting an OR to an RR. Let p₀ be the risk in the reference group and p₁ in the exposed. OR = [p₁/(1 − p₁)] ÷ [p₀/(1 − p₀)]. Solve for p₁ and divide by p₀:

RR = OR ÷ (1 − p₀ + p₀ × OR).

When p₀ is small, the denominator is close to 1 and RR ≈ OR. This is exact for a crude 2×2 table. Applied to an adjusted OR it is only approximate, and it can mislead in the CI (McNutt et al., 2003); use a model instead.

The sandwich, in the simplest case. Fit a Poisson model with only an intercept to n binary observations with x events. The MLE is b̂₀ = ln(x/n) = ln p̂. The Poisson model says Var(count) = mean, which gives SE(b̂₀) = 1/√x. But the observations are 0/1, so the true variance of p̂ is p̂(1 − p̂)/n (recall §7.2.2), and on the log scale SE(ln p̂) ≈ √[(1 − p̂)/(np̂)] = √[(1 − p̂)/x]. The ratio of the two is √(1 − p̂): the Poisson SE is too big by the factor 1/√(1 − p̂). The general sandwich SE replaces the model’s assumed variance with the squared residuals actually observed, (y − μ̂)², and “sandwiches” them between two copies of the inverse of the model’s information matrix (the curvature of the log-likelihood; the matrix algebra is beyond this book), which gives the method its name.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey, membership is 44.5% (69/155) among households whose mothers have secondary or higher education, and 18.5% (31/168) with no maternal education.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Crude PR = 0.445 ÷ 0.185 = 2.41. Crude OR = (69/86) ÷ (31/137) = 3.55. With a common outcome, the OR is almost 50% larger than the PR.
  2. Adjusted for distance and wealth (§13.3): OR = 1.87. Converted with the formula at p₀ = 0.185: 1.87 ÷ (1 − 0.185 + 0.185 × 1.87) = 1.61. The modified Poisson model gives PR 1.52 (95% CI 1.03 to 2.25).
  3. Sandwich SE for the overall prevalence (150/500): Poisson SE = 1/√150 = 0.0816; robust SE = √(0.70/150) = 0.0683, smaller by the factor √0.70 = 0.84.

blocks.alt: Odds ratios and prevalence ratios for the CBHI model
blocks.caption: Figure 13.3. The §13.3 model fitted twice to the same 500 households: logistic regression (odds ratios) and modified Poisson regression (prevalence ratios). Every OR lies further from 1 than the matching PR, because 30% of households are members.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(sandwich); library(lmtest)
# cb as in §13.3; modified Poisson
mp <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
            maternal_education, family = poisson, data = cb)
# robust SEs
coeftest(mp, vcov = vcovHC(mp, type = "HC0"))
round(exp(cbind(PR = coef(mp),
                coefci(mp, vcov = vcovHC(mp, type = "HC0")))), 2)
# log-binomial
lb <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
            maternal_education, family = binomial(link = "log"),
          data = cb)

wealth_index                  0.184159   0.039432  4.6703 3.007e-06 ***
maternal_educationprimary     0.215789   0.200784  1.0747  0.282495    
maternal_educationsecondary+  0.418499   0.199397  2.0988  0.035833 *  
...

vcovHC(type = "HC0") computes the sandwich variance; coeftest and coefci use it for the SEs, z-tests and CIs. Exponentiated, the coefficients are adjusted PRs: 0.95 per km (0.91 to 0.98), 1.20 per wealth unit, and 1.52 for secondary education (1.03 to 2.25). These are the orange points in Figure 13.3. The log-binomial model fails outright on these data. Supplied with starting values (start = c(log(0.3), 0, 0, 0, 0)), it runs but stops with “algorithm did not converge”, which is the practical problem McNutt et al. (2003) describe.

Marginal standardisation from the §13.3 logistic model:

m1 <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
            maternal_education, family = binomial, data = cb)
lev <- levels(cb$maternal_education)
d_sec <- transform(cb, maternal_education = factor("secondary+", lev))
d_non <- transform(cb, maternal_education = factor("none", lev))
p_sec <- mean(predict(m1, d_sec, type = "response"))
p_non <- mean(predict(m1, d_non, type = "response"))
round(c(p_secondary = p_sec, p_none = p_non,
        RR = p_sec / p_non, RD = p_sec - p_non), 3)
p_secondary      p_none          RR          RD 
      0.361       0.243       1.488       0.118

If every household had a mother with secondary education, the model predicts 36.1% membership; if none did, 24.3%. The standardised RR is 1.49, close to the modified-Poisson 1.52, and the risk difference is 11.8 percentage points.

points.html: Common outcome (more than about 10%) → report RR or PR, not only the OR. Cross-sectional → prevalence ratio; cohort → risk ratio.
Modified Poisson = Poisson family + log link + robust SE (Zou, 2004). Do not report its model-based SEs for binary data: they are too large.
Modified Poisson can predict probabilities above 1 for extreme households (one of 500 here, at 1.05). This does not bias the PRs much, but do not use the model to predict individual probabilities.
Log-binomial is the “proper” likelihood model but often fails to converge.
The OR → RR formula is exact only for a crude 2×2 table; for adjusted ORs use a model or marginal standardisation.
The robust SE here corrects the variance assumption, not clustering. Households in the same village are still correlated; §15.2.5 uses a clustered version of the same sandwich idea (GEE).

questions.prompt: In a cohort, 40% of unexposed people develop the outcome, and a crude OR is 2.0. Convert it to an RR. What would the RR be if the unexposed risk were 2%?
questions.answer: RR = OR ÷ (1 − p₀ + p₀ × OR). p₀ = 0.40: RR = 2.0 ÷ (1 − 0.40 + 0.80) = 2.0 ÷ 1.40 = 1.43. p₀ = 0.02: RR = 2.0 ÷ (1 − 0.02 + 0.04) = 2.0 ÷ 1.02 = 1.96. With a common outcome the OR of 2 corresponds to a much smaller RR; with a rare outcome the two almost coincide.

questions.prompt: Why does a Poisson model with a log link give valid prevalence ratios for a 0/1 outcome, and why must its SEs be replaced by robust ones?
questions.answer: The coefficients depend only on the model for the mean, log(p) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …, which is the prevalence-ratio model; the Poisson likelihood is used only as a working device to estimate it, and it gives consistent estimates when the mean model is right (Zou, 2004). But the Poisson model assumes Var(Y) = p, whereas a 0/1 outcome has Var(Y) = p(1 − p), which is smaller. The model-based SEs are therefore too large (by about 1/√(1 − p); for the CBHI prevalence of 30%, 0.0816 against the correct 0.0683). The robust (sandwich) SE uses the observed residuals instead of the assumed variance and corrects this.

questions.prompt: A colleague fits a log-binomial model and gets “algorithm did not converge”. Name two alternatives that still give an adjusted prevalence ratio.
questions.answer: 1. Modified Poisson regression: a Poisson model with a robust (sandwich) SE (Zou, 2004). (ii) Marginal standardisation from a logistic model: predict every person’s probability as if exposed and as if unexposed, average each, and take the ratio. (Supplying starting values to the log-binomial model sometimes helps but, as with the CBHI data, may still fail.)
